sentences.text: Coahuilaceratops magnacuerna is the only known species within the chasmosaurine subfamily.
Adults reached approximately 22 feet in length and stood 6 to 7 feet tall, weighing between four and five tons.
Its robust horns, which lack the constriction seen at the tips of some relatives, resemble those of Pentaceratops rather than Agujaceratops.
Despite incomplete remains, the animal is believed to have possessed some of the largest horns of any known dinosaur, rivaling those of Triceratops and Torosaurus.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists mainly of unarticulated skull bones from an adult, including horncores and parts of the frill.
Its horns are estimated to have been up to 1.2 meters long, rivaling those of Triceratops and Torosaurus.
Adults were estimated to be about 22 feet long, 6 to 7 feet tall, with a 6-foot skull and 3 to 4-foot horns, weighing four to five tons.
Fossils were discovered in 2001 and excavated in 2003 near Porvenir de Jalpa in Coahuila, Mexico.
Paleontologist Claudio De León found remains of two individuals, an adult and a juvenile, allowing the erection of the genus noted for its characteristic large horns.
The species was formally described in 2010 by a team of paleontologists including Mark A. Loewen and Scott D. Sampson, though it appeared as an informal nomen nudum in 2008.
It is the first dinosaur species described from the Cerro Huerta Formation.
The genus name derives from the toponym Coahuila.

Classification has varied; Loewen et al. (2010) placed it in a polytomy with Anchiceratops and Arrhinoceratops, forming a sister clade to Triceratopsini, while Brown & Henderson (2015) analyzed it as a sister genus to Bravoceratops within a clade of non-triceratopsin chasmosaurines.
Dalman et al. (2022) found it in a polytomy with Bravoceratops and Sierraceratops, suggesting this group was endemic to southern Laramidia.
It is considered the sister taxon to Bravoceratops, which was found in Texas, USA.
It lived in the Late Cretaceous, between 71 and 70 million years ago in the Maastrichtian, in what is now North America.
All specimens were collected from a single location in the middle layer of the Cerro Huerta Formation, dating to 71.5 to 70.5 million years ago.
